cells.name: Continuity and responsiveness
cells.example: T3 answers T2's imagination claim; T5 takes up T4's bad faith; T6 answers T5's structure.
cells.limitation: T9 ignores T7-T8 on commitment and capital, returning to the Stoic opening.

cells.name: Development of ideas
cells.example: T5 introduces habitus; T8 builds on it with choosing different forms of capital.
cells.limitation: T6 and T9 restate the Stoic opening; habitus is never used to test the user's not-wanting.

cells.name: Exploration of central tensions
cells.example: T3-T6 examine agency versus social structure versus detachment.
cells.limitation: Nobody raises drifting friendships or the chance the user does want these milestones.

cells.name: Integration of perspectives
cells.example: T8 partly folds T7's commitment into Bourdieu's field: choose other capital.
cells.limitation: No mind qualifies its own view; Stoic position at T9 identical to T2.

cells.name: Progress toward understanding
cells.example: Section D sharpens the open question: detach from status or choose other values.
cells.limitation: Section D largely restates the three opening positions rather than a narrowed question.

cells.name: Faithful engagement
cells.example: T5 represents T4's bad faith fairly before adding habitus.
cells.limitation: T6 answers T5 as if structure were optional, ignoring that habitus shapes desires.

cells.name: Substance of challenges
cells.example: T5 names T4's assumption: you can think your way out of structure.
cells.limitation: T6 restates detachment instead of answering T5; T7's objection to T6 goes unanswered.

cells.name: Accuracy and support
cells.example: T2 paraphrases Seneca's Letter 13 accurately; T5 uses habitus correctly.
cells.limitation: Minds list dates Letters from a Stoic, a modern anthology title, as 65.

cells.name: Calibration and transparency
cells.example: T3 frames feeling behind as a rational response, a hedged interpretation.
cells.limitation: T1 asserts the user copies scripts to avoid freedom; T2 asserts what disturbs them.

cells.name: Intellectual honesty and revision
cells.example: T8 partly accepts T4/T7's point that a different path can be chosen.
cells.limitation: No mind concedes anything across nine turns; T5's habitus objection never conceded by Stoic.

cells.name: Identification of the actual concern
cells.example: Section A names the gap between not wanting milestones and still feeling behind.
cells.limitation: Ambiguity whether the user truly does not want these things is never explored.

cells.name: Meaningful use of personal context
cells.example: T9 uses the house: needing it to prove you are not behind.
cells.limitation: Friends' milestones appear only as generic examples; no detail changes any argument.

cells.name: Fit with goals and values
cells.example: T8 suggests valuing other capital, matching the user's doubt about milestones.
cells.limitation: T7 imposes Sartre's commit-or-drift value rather than the user's stated uncertainty.

cells.name: Attention to constraints and stakes
cells.example: Section E mentions finding a community that values the chosen path.
cells.limitation: Friendships changing, timing and money stakes never addressed in any turn.

cells.name: Responsiveness to information
cells.example: Section E branches on lack of purpose versus fear of exclusion, each with implication.
cells.limitation: No question asks whether the user might want these later or what behind measures.

cells.name: Clarification of desires and motivations
cells.example: Section E offers purpose-lack and exclusion-fear as alternative sources of discomfort.
cells.limitation: T1 declares avoidance of freedom as the user's hidden motive.

cells.name: Examination of assumptions
cells.example: T2 surfaces the judgment that house and marriage are necessary for a good life.
cells.limitation: The user's assumption that they do not want these things is never examined.

cells.name: Clarification of values and priorities
cells.example: T8 contrasts property and family with intellectual or creative capital.
cells.limitation: Belonging versus authenticity named in D but the user's own priorities never elicited.

cells.name: Recognition of fears and outside expectations
cells.example: T3 treats feeling behind as rational, not a flaw; E names fear of exclusion.
cells.limitation: T9's slave-to-opinions line edges toward judging the user's feeling.

cells.name: Agency and reflective ownership
cells.example: Section E gives branches the user can test against their own discomfort.
cells.limitation: T4 and T7 issue verdicts (bad faith, merely drifting) rather than open distinctions.

cells.name: Definition of the decision and options
cells.example: Section E frames defining a new project versus building a community.
cells.limitation: The decision faced is never stated; waiting or wanting milestones later not options.

cells.name: Explanation of tradeoffs
cells.example: T8 notes you cannot opt out of the social field entirely.
cells.limitation: No cost named for opting out (friendships, status) or opting in.

cells.name: Identification of decisive conditions
cells.example: Section E: purpose-lack favours a new project; exclusion-fear favours community.
cells.limitation: Conditions are introspective labels, nothing the user could observe or count.

cells.name: Treatment of uncertainty
cells.example: Section E allows an if-you-remain-unsure branch.
cells.limitation: Consequential unknowns, like whether wants may change, never separated from minor ones.

cells.name: Proportionate next steps
cells.example: Section E proposes a small independent goal to test the feeling.
cells.limitation: The goal is unspecified and does not follow from any turn's argument.

cells.name: Accessible language
cells.example: T9 states the core idea plainly: needing the house to prove something.
cells.limitation: T5 habitus and T8 forms of capital used without plain explanation.

cells.name: Traceable arguments and references
cells.example: T6 'The structure' clearly points to T5; T4 'the system' to T3.
cells.limitation: T9's seek-or-reject-status opener answers no identifiable turn.

cells.name: Manageable pacing and turn length
cells.example: Nine turns, all within the word range, readable in one pass.
cells.limitation: Turns are near-uniform in length, giving a metronomic rhythm.

cells.name: Distinguishable positions and voices
cells.example: Positions distinct: freedom (T1), detachment (T2), structure (T3).
cells.limitation: All three share one lecturing register; no explicit change of position anywhere.

cells.name: Economy and sustained attention
cells.example: Turns are compact with little filler.
cells.limitation: T6 and T9 repeat T2's Stoic point about externals with little new.

cells.name: Meaningful stakes and tension
cells.example: T3 versus T2: is the pressure imagined or a real status system?
cells.limitation: Stakes stay abstract; the user's friendships and life never put at risk.

cells.name: Surprise and reversals
cells.example: T8 mildly surprises by joining choice to Bourdieu's field.
cells.limitation: No reversal occurs; every mind ends where it began.

cells.name: Personality and expressive voice
cells.example: T9 Stoic's slave-to-opinions line has Seneca's edge.
cells.limitation: Voices are flat textbook summaries in one shared declarative register.

cells.name: Memorable delivery
cells.example: T1: life as a finished product you failed to assemble.
cells.limitation: Few images beyond T1; no examples drawn from the user's situation.

cells.name: Anticipation and emotional movement
cells.example: T3's defence of the feeling briefly shifts tone from rebuke to validation.
cells.limitation: Constant didactic intensity across T1-T9; no build or release.

strengths: T5 Social Critic's habitus objection names a real assumption in T4 and develops the debate.
T3 validates feeling behind as rational rather than pathologising the user.
Section E offers two alternative sources of discomfort as conditional branches.
weaknesses: No mind concedes or revises across T1-T9; the Stoic ends at T9 where T2 began.
T1 Existentialist and T2 Stoic assert the user's motives and judgments as fact.
The user's situation is used generically; friendships, timing and tradeoffs never enter any turn.

symptoms.observed: Stoic never concedes T5's habitus point; repeats detachment unchanged.
symptoms.evidence: The structure only has power if you grant it importance.

symptoms.observed: User's motive and judgment stated as fact, not offered as possibility.
symptoms.evidence: so you look to your friends' scripts to avoid the burden

symptoms.observed: Friends' milestones stay generic; no effect on friendships or timing discussed.
symptoms.evidence: These milestones are social signals that define your place

symptoms.observed: No mind changes position; ending mirrors openings.
symptoms.evidence: Whether you seek status or reject it, the goal remains

symptoms.observed: Choosing other capital offered with no stated cost.
symptoms.evidence: you can choose to value different forms of capital

findings.description: Runner flagged one pd=false turn with quotation marks; the only candidate seen is the plural possessive apostrophe in friends' scripts, not a quotation.
As I once wrote, we suffer more in imagination than in reality closely paraphrases Seneca Letter 13; appears faithful, no quotation marks.
Letters from a Stoic is a modern anthology title, listed with the date 65; the letters themselves date to about 65 AD.

rubric_fit_notes: The deterministic check reports one pd=false turn with quotation marks, but reading T1, T3, T4, T5, T7 and T8 I find only the plural possessive in T1 (friends' scripts), which the brief says is not a quotation mark; I therefore record no cap. If the runner saw a character I cannot, the cap would apply. The self_reflection subtype sits awkwardly with decision-oriented C5 cells; I read the decision as how to respond to the feeling of being behind.
question_type_note: Read as a decision of the self_reflection kind, so C5 was judged on how to respond to feeling behind rather than a concrete life choice.
